title: Mountain Climbing Down in Japan's Bear-Hit Regions
paragraphs: Japan's mountains are popular with hikers, especially in spring and autumn. However, new data suggests that fewer people are climbing mountains in parts of the country where bears have become a serious problem.

The data comes from Beacon Bank, a company that analyzes how people move using GPS data from smartphones. It looked at the number of people near the tops of Japan's "100 Famous Mountains," a list created by a Japanese mountaineer in 1964. The company compared the period from April to June in 2024, 2025 and 2026. It chose spring because bears are very active after they wake up from their winter sleep.

Across Japan, the share of climbers fell by 18% compared with 2024. The biggest drop was in the Tohoku region in northern Japan, where the number of climbers fell by 34% over two years. Of the 23 mountains with the most reliable data, Mount Hachimantai, in Iwate Prefecture in Tohoku, saw the largest decrease, at 46%. On the other hand, Mount Kaimon, in Kagoshima in southern Japan, saw an increase of 18%.

Tohoku has had more bear sightings than any other region since 2022. According to Japan's Ministry of the Environment, there were 50,801 bear sightings in Tohoku in 2025, compared with 20,513 in 2023. The number rose sharply in autumn 2025, after a poor harvest of acorns and nuts pushed hungry bears into towns. Between April 2025 and March 2026, bears attacked more than 200 people across Japan, and 13 people died.

According to Beacon Bank, the pattern is "geographically consistent." However, the data does not prove that bears are the reason for the decline, and other factors may also be involved. Some local people may simply be avoiding the mountains to be safe.
Experts advise hikers in Japan to carry bear spray and bells and to check information about bear sightings before climbing.
